paras: The attempted lynching of Alberti Rossi took place on May 18, 1888, at Browntown, a suburb of 'Pittown' (also printed 'Pittson'), Pennsylvania, when a crowd of men and boys hanged an Italian railroad worker from a tree. Rossi, accused of attacking three girls, was lowered alive when some of the men interfered.

According to a Wilkes-Barre dispatch dated May 19, three young girls looking for stray cows in the woods were seized by three Italians working on a new Lehigh Valley Railroad branch to Laurel Run. The girls resisted and screamed, and were bruised and had their clothing torn. Their screams drew Peter Mulderig, a miner on his way to work, and the Italians fled when he ran to the girls and took them home to Browntown.

Once the girls' story spread, a crowd of men and boys set out after the Italians, in the dispatch's words "bent on a desperate revenge." They found the accused men with other Italians at one of the workers' shanties and attacked them, and a fight with knives, clubs and rocks followed in which "many wounds were inflicted."

When the Italians scattered, the crowd caught Rossi, whom the dispatch named as one of the girls' attackers. A rope was put round his neck and thrown over a tree limb, and he was swung off his feet while he begged for mercy. Some of the men then had him lowered; he was unconscious but not seriously hurt.
No report of arrests, charges against the crowd, or charges against Rossi or the other accused men appears in the coverage.

The only account found ran a week after the event in The Columbian of Bloomsburg, Pennsylvania, on May 25, 1888, under the headlines "Strung Up For a Lynching" and "An Infuriated Pennsylvania Mob Nearly Hang an Italian." The dispatch presented the girls' account as fact, referred to the Italians as "foreigners" and "their kind," and called Rossi one of those who had assaulted the girls. It also described the crowd as "excited and bloodthirsty" and credited the "better sense" of the men who stopped the hanging.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Alberti Rossi
bases: A crowd hunted down Italian railroad workers accused of attacking three girls, fought them, and hanged one, Alberti Rossi, from a tree before some of the men had him lowered (A1).

A crowd of men and boys, acting without lawful authority in revenge for an alleged assault, hanged Rossi, but he was lowered and was reported unconscious and not seriously hurt, so no one was killed (A1).
The only report found is one Wilkes-Barre dispatch printed in the Bloomsburg Columbian (A1).

accounts.label: Wire report (Wilkes-Barre dispatch)
accounts.gist: Three Italians attacked three girls, who were rescued by a miner; a crowd then attacked the Italians at their shanty and nearly hanged Rossi before some of the men had him lowered.

framing.detail: The dispatch treats the assault as established, calls the Italians 'foreigners' and 'their kind', but describes the crowd as 'excited and bloodthirsty' and credits the 'better sense' of the men who stopped the hanging.

record_check.dossier: The article prints the name 'Alberti Rossi'.
Italian; the papers do not otherwise give race.
Fighting with knives, clubs and rocks, and hanging; no one is reported killed.
Browntown, a suburb printed as 'Pittown' and 'Pittson' in the same article.
A crowd of men and boys from Browntown, none named.
